Mr. Speaker, for a moment or two I should like to touch on the tourist industry; as usual, my subjects are non-partisan. When I spoke in this house during my first session here, in 1945, I urged the desirability of greater recognition of what I thought was our greatest potential industry in this country; that is, the tourist industry. At that time I suggested that this industry warranted a cabinet minister without too many other responsibilities. I believe it is the opinion of many that this would be most desirable. At the moment it does not seem the tourist bureau is doing justice to what we have to offer in this country, and I would suggest to the government that there are other ways in which this industry might be stimulated. They might have a deputy minister to look after it, or they might have a commission. Those provinces which are paying a great deal of attention to that industry are benefiting from their efforts. If we could have a tourist commission representative of all the provinces, which would be a permanent body, it could more or less correlate the work necessary really to promote the industry. We have representatives of the Department of Trade and Commerce in all parts of the world to develop our export trade, but I think many hon. members will agree that we are not taking advantage of what we in this country have to offer by way of attractions for tourists.
When I spoke in 1945 I said we had and would continue to have a need for United States dollars, and this is one way in which we can obtain those dollars without exporting goods. Instead, we have emissaries of good will who go back to their own country and bring more tourists here. At that time I think I showed that all segments of our society benefit from this industry. Everyone, no matter how he may derive his income, benefits. Of course we did not try to promote this industry during the war, but the war has been over for two or three years, and I think it will be generally agreed that some lead should now be given by the government to co-ordinate the work of the different provinces, because it is to the benefit of all. At that time I illustrated what I had in mind by a little story. Nine men sat down to a table which was covered with good things to eat. Their arms were tied in such a way that they could not raise their forks or spoons to their own mouths. They solved that problem by having each man feed the person to his left. If the

The Address-Mr. Murphy
dominion and the provinces could co-operate in somewhat the same way it would increase our supply of the much required United States dollars and benefit all.
I have had some returns brought down by the department in connection with this industry, and from them I see that most of the money to be spent on the development of this industry has been spent on advertising. I am not quarreling with the way in which the money has been spent; I believe the department should have more money for other purposes, and I also believe that if we had some government leadership such as those indicated, more attention would be given to this industry. For instance, in a return brought down just the other day I notice that last year the travel bureau under the Department of Trade and Commerce spent $768,000, of which $618,000 was for advertising. If we are in business we know that if we have a good product to sell we must certainly advertise it. I for one believe that if more attention were given the tourist industry our revenue from that source would increase immeasurably. According to the same return, I notice that total expenditures in Canada by United States citizens was $214,000,000 in 1946. I see no reason why we should not develop this industry to the point where these tourists will spend a billion dollars annually. We have everything to offer, even more than Switzerland, where the tourist industry is practically the only source of income.
I suggest to the minister now in charge of this department that steps should be taken to promote this industry. I believe one way of doing so would be in connection with films we get from Hollywood. We could arrange a barter. We might have films made in each province of Canada and, in addition to the advertising we do in United States publications, by means of this barter we could have these films shown throughout the United States, advertising our scenery and natural playgrounds. I notice also, according to this return, that the only person in that bureau who speaks on these matters in the United States is the director himself, whereas I believe they might well have ten, fifteen or twenty speakers travelling through the United States, speaking to service clubs and other organizations and we would be well rewarded. The first people these Americans meet when they enter our country are very important to them, because the first impression is usually the one that lasts. I should like to pay tribute to the customs and immigration officials we have in our employ in the Dominion of Canada. They 5849-78
are courteous and efficient. I believe the department should give careful consideration to the wages or remuneration these men are receiving, in view of the duties and responsibilities they have to perform.
In all fairness to these employees, the department should consider what United States immigration and customs officials are getting, because we on the border-and this applies to all border points-have Canadian customs and immigration officials going into the United States and coming back to the border by train. Then, we have United States customs and immigration officials coming into Canada, and returning to the border. On those same trains are either American or Canadian engineers and conductors. If we make a comparison I believe we shall find that the remuneration of these railway employees compares favourably with each other, and I suggest that there should also be a fair comparison between the pay received by Canadian customs and immigration officials and that received by those employed by the United States.
I regret to say that a comparison of pay between Canadian and American customs and immigration officials at the present time does not disclose that our officials are as well paid. I have not time to give details of figures, but I want the house to know that these men are not drawing much more than 60 per cent of the amounts drawn by United States customs and immigration officials; yet they are doing the same work. I do hope that these men will receive the consideration they deserve.
In the next few minutes I should like to deal on a non-partisan basis, with the Veterans Land Act, and the general subject of VLA housing. However, before going into details of what I purpose saying I should like through you, Mr. Speaker, to express to the new Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg) the wish that the people of this country will have as high a regard for his administration of the department as they have for his honour in achieving such a splendid war record.
What I have to say is factual. I appreciate that the present minister was not in the government until recently, and I trust that he will not take as a personal attack any criticism which I may have to offer, because I shall be fair in what I have to say. May I also emphasize my high regard for the deputy minister of veterans affairs, a man who holds the respct and good will of veterans throughout the country. It seems to me that the
The Address-Mr. Murphy

administration of the Veterans Land Act may be the only blot on the department; and I believe I am expressing not only the wish of veterans, but that of many other people when I say that I hope the department will now endeavour to correct the injustices which the veterans justly allege, and which I allege, have been perpetrated on them in the past.
In order that there may be no misunderstanding, let me point out that on February 4, 1947, I spoke in the house and demanded a royal commission. After having recited certain particulars, which have since been verified to the satisfaction of a great many people, I said:
I demand that a royal commission be appointed to inquire into all contracts for purchases of land acquired for small holdings under the Veterans Land Act, to inquire into all contracts for the building of homes for veterans under the Veterans Land Act and contracts for the construction of roads the installation of water mains and other costs involved in the purchase of these homes.
I repeat that demand tonight. And I am going to add to the demand for a royal commission the request that it inquire into the administration of the Veterans Land Act. I hope the few remarks I shall have to make will warrant the government's granting this demand.
When on that occasion I asked for a royal commission, we did not know as much as we later learned; and certainly did not know what we know today. I sincerely believe we were entitled to a royal commission at that time; and certainly I believe today-and there can be no question about the sincerity of my belief-that the veterans of this country are entitled to a royal commission to inquire into the facts of the matters the investigation of which I have sought.
It must be borne in mind that these veterans were young lads without homes. They wanted homes as badly as did other people, and most certainly they were more entitled to them than were many others who had them. In all fairness to the government, I must say that it did provide roofs over the heads of these veterans, and provided them at low monthly payments. I would be most unfair if I were to rise in my place in the house and say otherwise.
I should like to bring the house up to date on what has happened. In the first place, I entered this scrap for no political purpose. I entered it on behalf of the veterans; and I have told them that when they are satisfied I will quit, and that I will not quit before they have had a fair deal. At this time I should like to pay tribute where tribute is due. I do not think we would have had this

matter before the public accounts committee, where so much information was revealed with respect to what has already taken place had it not been for the support of the press across this country. And in this connection I pay special tribute to the press of western Ontario including the Windsor Star, the Sarnia Observer, the London Free Press and many others. At this moment I should like to pay special tribute to one who is most responsible for the matter being brought thus far. As a matter of fact, he is now in the press gallery, and is none other than the representative of the Windsor Star, who brought this matter to my attention in January, 1947.
As the house knows, I was approached in January by some veterans who had received an ultimatum from the department, and the particulars of that ultimatum were recited by me at that time. They were told that either they would agree to buy their homes within a week or they could stay in until May 1 and pay rent, but by the end of May they would have to vacate. I investigated the houses, but I shall not recite now what I found out. Hon. members will recall the details I gave in February, 1947, and can read what came before the public accounts committee. Along with contractors I investigated these houses in Sarnia and Windsor and I am prepared to say that I advised the veterans to seek a new contract. I thought, and I think everyone who is fair will agree with me, that they were entitled to that. I think I should take this opportunity to say that the veterans are grateful for the support they received from other hon. members on this side of the house in their demand for a royal commission.
At that time I was not aware that there were other areas in Canada as bad as either of these two areas, but it was afterwards admitted before the public accounts committee by the director of the Veterans Land Act that other areas were just as bad as Sarnia, which, of course, was terrible. He referred to such places as Sackville, New Brunswick; Boucher-ville, Quebec; and Braefoot, British Columbia, as being in the same category.
I think it was on March 3, 1947, that the veterans in these areas who had not signed up received another ultimatum which was dated Toronto, March 3, 1947. This is set out on page 529 of the proceedings of the public accounts committee and it reads in part:
This application was signed by you in the presence of a commissioner for taking affidavits and the department can only assume that you completed this document in the best of faith.
In spite of the above, you refuse to sign the agreement of sale which was presented to you in the course of the past few days, and in view

The Address-Mr. Murphy
of this, the department has no alternative but to take steps to make the home in which you are presently residing, available to another veteran who is agreeable to completing the agreements presented.
And further down:
If however, you still are not prepared to sign, you may vacate the premises within one week from the date shown on the letterhead.
The former minister of veterans affairs gave his assurance in this house that the veterans would not be asked to sign purchase contracts until the repairs were made. The repairs had not even been started when authority was given to send out that ultimatum. I sometimes wonder if the director of the Veterans Land Act did not assume too much. I have stated publicly on different occasions that I did1 not think the Minister of Veterans Affairs or his deputy were aware of what was taking place with respect to these various ultimatums. When I see the amounts that have been spent in administering the Veterans Land Act I realize that somebody must assume responsibility in all V.L.A. matters and, of course, that must be the government. In view of the assurances which had been given by the minister on the floor of this house, I make no apology for having advised these veterans not to sign.
Immediately after that the deputy minister of veterans affairs and two others visited these homes, and in fact I -was in Sarnia when they came there. They saw the houses for themselves and the deputy minister was kind enough to assure the veterans that they would not be obliged to sign contracts until repairs had been made. Then, a royal commission not being set up, the matter was brought before the public accounts committee. One reason I suggested a royal commission is that, while this matter might be brought before the public accounts committee, our experience last summer showed that it would take hundreds of hours to hear the evidence of the complaints from the different areas. I submit that these veterans are entitled to have their cases reviewed by some tribunal.
When the public accounts committee was dealing with this matter, it took some four or five sittings of the committee to elaborate upon the details of faulty construction I had given the house. That is why I say that the public accounts committee could not go into the complaints from all these projects across the country. That committee served1 a useful purpose, and I should like to quote one or two recommendations it made, as reported on page 708 of the minutes of the public accounts committee for 1947. They are:

evidence by veterans of other projects. Your committee hopes that remedial measures taken as a result of its report may satisfactorily adjust defects which may have occurred in other projects.

Your committee recommends that a board of three men be appointed consisting of real estate and building experts, none of whom shall have had previous connection with the Department of Veterans Affairs, or with any other governmental building projects, to pursue the work undertaken by your committee, with a view to giving justice and fair treatment to veteran purchasers and all parties interested in this question. and to recommend to the minister any remedy it may consider fit to correct the situation.

I attended a meeting at the request of the veterans in Windsor as a result of that ultimatum, and I assured them that this could not be action that the minister or the deputy minister would take. Some repairs had been made, but not completed. I shall refer now to a return tabled in the house
The Address-Mr. Murphy

last year. This is further evidence to corroborate the necessity for a royal commission. I quote from sessional paper No. 1351, in reply to questions I asked. I shall quote only one question:
What was the cost per unit overhead and liow was the same made up?
The answer was:
Average per unit at Sarnia, $1,736.22.
Before giving the remainder of the answer to that question, let me say, so that there may be no doubt about it, that we discovered, before the public accounts committee, that the houses at Sarnia cost the department $10,106 and, may I say, they are still not completed. The drainage work has still to be done. With the additional work to be done and administration overhead, the cost of all houses built under V.L.A. will probably be in excess of $11,000 or $12,000.
I now will give the remainder of the answer to question No. 6, to which I have just referred.
Project overhead includes the following items:
Temporary buildings, salaries of staff located on the project including superintendents, accountants, bookkeepers, stenographers, timekeepers, material checkers, first aid attendant, watchman, and water boys-*
Water boys for eight houses! One water boy was not sufficient. It goes on:
-miscellaneous expenses incurred at job office in direct relation to the project include travelling expenses, telegrams, and telephone calls.
I inquired what the unit overhead cost was in Windsor but have not .vet received that information, nor have we received answers to many other questions placed on the order paper regarding the project overhead or the .unit overhead of various projects.
Another return -was tabled last fall, 135F, in reply to questions asked by the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Stephenson). The question asked was:
What has been the total cost for administration of the V.L.A. from its inception up to February 28, 1947?
The answer to that question is given in the return:
Approximately $8,903,000. To some extent the same staff is engaged in Soldier Settlement and Veterans Land Act and other work on which the administration is engaged. The figure given is a close estimate, and includes $331,256.93 for legal fees and $563,568.50 for taxes.
I contend, Mr. Speaker, that in view of the evidence before the public accounts committee, and evidence such as I have given here tonight, and the concrete evidence of the construction itself and the admission by the director of V.L.A. and by the minister and

the deputy minister of defects in construction, the careless supervision and huge amounts spent by the director of V.L.A. for administration purposes, we should certainly inquire how that money was spent and how the administration of the Veterans Land Act spent the moneys allocated to them.
We know there is going to be depreciation in homes, and the more badly the home is constructed, the greater the depreciation There is the probability of gradual declines in home values, beginning three or four years hence, if not before, on well-built homes. On poorly constructed homes the decline in value and the depreciation will be much greater.
The director of V.L.A. admitted that these houses were of poor construction, and not only these but the others to which I have referred. I say here that the veterans are entitled to an opportunity to enjoy decent well-built homes at fair prices. The government has defaulted in its obligation to carry out this principle. Inflationary factors in the current situation arising from liberal credits and from other governmental policies are such as to keep the potential demand high in relation to housing supply, and for that reason the government let it be known that many veterans now without homes will be glad to move into these homes.
The minister stated, as reported at page 589 of Hansard-and I am not going to deal harshly with his statements-that these defects were inevitable. I contend, in view of the evidence we had submitted to us, and it is obvious to anyone who has inspected these houses, that there was no occasion for them to have had these defects, and I am sure the minister will agree that is in fact the case. As reported at page 589 of Hansard he said:
When the defects became apparent, my predecessor said on the floor of the house that the houses would be placed in first-class condition at no cost to the veteran.
We appreciate that. Yet the veterans were asked to sign contracts before the repairs were made and the repairs are even yet not complete.
In the few minutes I have left I want to compare cost of other houses with these V.L.A. houses. We know that a committee of three valuators has given a valuation on these veterans' homes. I said a moment ago that the public accounts committee recommended that none of those chosen as valuators should have been in any way connected with government building projects; but I understand, although it does not prejudice me in my thinking, that one of these valuators did build several hundred or about a thousand homes as a government project.

The Address-Mr. Murphy
I am going to compare the prices of a recently completed project in the Toronto area with these V.L.A. homes. These homes in Toronto area are of solid brick, constructed at 1947 prices, and the houses are just completed. The houses have 18,000 cubic feet and are from 10 to 15 per cent larger than the ones built under the V.L.A. The V.L.A. used the same nine or ten plans all across the country. The cost of this project in the Toronto area for home, excluding land, is $5,280; that is, without the upstairs being completed. These houses were of brick construction, with basements, hardwood floors, excellent kitchens, hot air heating, built-in baths, built-in cupboards in the kitchens, tile floors in the kitchens, plastered walls, and are completed in a satisfactory manner; much better homes than the V.L.A. homes.
In view of the fact that the minister referred to the new valuation of these houses I did wish to compare the prices.

I thank you for that courtesy, Mr. Speaker. The valuations that were made by this committee were made last December. The houses were under construction in 1945, and I think the house will agree with me that in that period the cost of construction had increased some twenty-five per cent at the very least. I believe the government figures will show that the increase in building costs are much higher for that period. I regret to say this, but it is nevertheless necessary that I should, because the minister in his statement emphasized that the valuators had never seen the prices previously quoted by the Veterans Land Act administration. He said, as reported at page 590 of Hansard:
I want to make it absolutely clear that this independent appraisal committee set their prices without any reference to the prices previously quoted by the Veterans Land Act administration. They did not have in their possession the prices which the veterans had originally been asked for the houses.
I do not say this unkindly of the minister; I think he will appreciate that. I shall deal with the Sarnia area first. I want to call the attention of the house to the fact that the reduction in valuation ran from some $853 to
$1,619 per house. The over-all reduction was $1 ,228 per house. I must also refer briefly to some two or three of the valuations of the Windsor area rather than give the figures. The information is available in the report which the minister tabled. On a great many of the houses there was a difference of only a few dollars, $10, $12, $15 and $25 which would indicate to me, or to anyone else, that this committee certainly must have had this report, because it is almost physically and mentally impossible for valuators to valuate one hundred houses and come within $10 $15, $20 or $25 of the price which the government had set as the price to the veterans. In fact the prices charged to the veterans were available to the public.
I wish to say, in fairness to the minister, that he has provided the veterans with an opportunity of renting if they so desire. I maintain that these veterans really have to buy these houses. I do not blame them for buying them, because they can have them at a low monthly payment, and by buying them they have a roof over their heads. They are more or less forced into it. They are tired out. They have had so many investigators and inspectors around that many of them have decided to buy and take their medicine.
In conclusion, I am going to say this. I have the authority of my leader to tell this house that if these veterans do not get justice from this government, and if we are fortunate enough to form the next government and I expect we shall, we shall review and revalue-these houses and see that the veterans get the-justice that this government denied them.
When I began my remarks I asked for a royal commission. I want to repeat that. I think we are entitled to it and, on behalf of these veterans, I expect that this government will grant the royal commission.

Mr. Speaker, to me this has been the most interesting session that I have attended since I became a member. We are living in troubled times. The papers carry such contradictory headlines as, ''spiraling prices", ''crashing prices of commodities", and such headlines as I found in the February 3 issue of the Vancouver Sun on the editorial page, "Homeless, workless, hungry", in speaking of the plight of the single unemployed of Vancouver, which has been becoming worse each year since the war ended. In part it says:
Neither explanations nor regrets ever put a meal in a man's stomach or a pillow under his head.
Some of the attitudes expressed by various members of the government have been good,.
The Address-Mr. Archibald

but some, I believe, are due for criticism. The February 9 issue of Time magazine quotes an interview that some housewives had with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) protesting the high cost of living.
When one of the ladies said she had eight children Mr. Abbott cracked, "You must do pretty well out of the family allowance."
When he was on his visit to the United States in order to obtain the $300 million loan he gave a press interview in which he spoke of Canada's austerity program. He spoke about the nutritious value found in home-grown beets and turnips. I can see that, from a business angle, that was a good approach. There he was, going to our masters on Wall street asking for a loan, and in this interview he said, "Look gentlemen, I can drive the standard of the Canadian people down to that of the eastern European peasant and make them like it. You can easily give me a loan. I can exploit it out of the Canadian people." The hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) has a solution. He goes one better than Marie Antoinette who told us to eat cake when we had no bread. "The hon. member for Vancouver North now [DOT]wants to put margarine on the cake.
The attitude expressed by the minister may *sound glib; it may sound cynical. I would [DOT]suggest that if he wants to take that attitude "Some day he give us the diet of that great liberal figure who discovered the nutritional value of ordinary lawn grass, Nebuchadnezzar. He might as well make it ridiculous and be done with it.
Let us see what is actually happening in the realm of action by the government in its handling of costs that have to do with the standard of the working classes. I hold in my hand correspondence from local 360 of the International Brotherhood of Papermakers, Ocean Falls, in which they inform me that the company, Pacific Mills, asked the rentals control board to send one of their administrators because they wished to raise the rents. Mr. Lobley went up for the department. He stayed there for two days and interviewed about twenty tenants out of a total of about five hundred, and then he left.
According to the information from local 360, rents are to be raised from two per cent to forty-eight per cent, with an average rise of twenty-four per cent. I wrote a protest to Mr. W. L. A. Pope, deputy administrator, rentals administration of the wartime prices and trade board, Ottawa, over the matter, because I thought that if an administrator were to go into any ordinary community and take a Gallup poll of the people and then 
raise all rents because he had interviewed twenty persons, there would be a howl and we would hear about individual justice. But because he went to a company town he took it for what he thought it was by his attitude, a slave compound, and once he got a crosssection of it he let it go at that.

Houses

What the hon. member wants to do is to stamp them all in the same mould. But he will not make that stick.
In answer to my protest I received a letter from Mr. Pope, and this is what he said:
For your information I enclose herewith a copy of the decision made by Mr. Owen Lobley, which you will notice is approved by Mr. K. W. Taylor, chairman of the wartime prices and trade board.
This decision is self-explanatory.
I am going to put this decision on the record. I may say that this document is something marvellous to read:
Rentals Administration,
4!>0 Sussex street. Ottawa.
In the matter of the housing accommodation situated at the place known as Ocean Falls, in the province of British Columbia, of which accommodation Pacific Mills Limited is the landlord, employees of the landlord are the tenants:
Whereas the landlord has requested me to increase the maximum rentals of the said accommodations by the exercise of the discretionary power vested in me;
Whereas I have heard the representatives and representations of the landlord and the tenants;
Considering that all the land and buildings of every kind situated at Ocean Falls are the property of Pacific Mills Limited;
Considering that all places of dwelling at Ocean Falls have been constructed by Pacific Mills Limited for the accommodation of its employees because no one else would provide this accommodation-
No one else would provide the accommodation! Have you ever tried to put up a building in a company town? It is a physical impossibility. Even the legion there had to fight to put up their own building. Perhaps the only building that is not owned by the company is the post office, and sometimes I wonder if it is not owned by them. To continue:
Considering that the leases of the employee-tenants of these accommodations can be terminated under the provisions of the laws of the province of British Columbia, and that the ter-

The Address-Mr. Archibald
mination of these leases is not affected by the orders of the wartime prices and trade board;
Considering that in this community the amounts deducted from the tenant-employee's pay in consideration for the living quarters provided for him by his employer cannot cause inflation, nor can it affect the housing shortage in Canada: -
That is a fundamental statement.
Considering that the amount of rental-deductions from the pay of the respective employees in the said community is not related to the purposes and objects of Canadian rent control-
Now here it is:
Now therefore, I, Owen Lobley, rentals administrator, by virtue of the power vested in me, do hereby exempt all accommodations situated in the place known as Ocean Falls, in the province of British Columbia, from the provisions of order number 294 of the wartime prices and trade board as amended.
Dated at Ottawa, this 5th dav of February, 1948.
Who is this egotistical, stupid, frustrated little man who is taking on himself the power of royalty dispensing largesse? I read this order number 294, and the only institutions I could find that could escape the laws of this dominion were religious institutions and1 institutions given to charity. I do not believe that anybody in British Columbia could possibly call the Pacific Mills a charitable or a religious institution; yet this little man takes all that power in his hands and this is foisted on these workers, whether they like it or not.
I have never in this house criticized the civil service because I believe they are doing a good job; but there is a limit, and this is the limit, and that is one action that the government is going ahead with.
I should like to give some other actions of the government by way of comparison. Let me state some of their actions in the last few years.
In the realm of taxation, on April 29, 1947, there came out in the budget an income tax reduction of $12 for married men with an income of $1,600.
On April 28, 1947, in the same budget, there was an income tax reduction of $733 for a married man with an income of $10,000.
Take another comparison. On May 27, 1947, the government voted down the C.C.F. proposal to raise the income tax exemptions to $1,000 for single men and $2,000 for married men.
On December 31, 1947, the government completely removed the corporation excess profits tax.
On June 1, 1946, the governmnet subsidy of two cents a quart on milk was removed. On
October 1, 1946, the government subsidy of fifty-five cents per hundredweight on milk was removed.
On February 14, 1947, there was a contract signed retroactive to January 1, 1946, to provide a subsidy of $7,200,000 in 1947-48 to Dosco on steel production, the same to Algoma, granting a subsidy of $1,600,000 and lesser amounts to other corporations.
In 1947 the government gave $400,000 to Crane Limited as an incentive bonus.
This government, you know, does not believe in subsidies, but you have to watch it. It is like Peter. It denies more than three times the thing it has faith in.
On July 17, 1947, they failed to pay the cost of living bonus suggested by the C.C.F. to superannuated civil servants, who in many cases receive less than the old age pension.
On June 30. 1946, gold mines whose profit margin was 84 an ounce or less were exempted from tax.
On July 30. 1946, the bill to tax co-operatives was passed.
On August 17, 1946, Bill No. 250 to increase the pay of judges to $20,000 was passed.
On July 7, 1947, a bill was passed to provide diplomats with pensions up to $7,000 a year for life.

Oh, no. I want to finish my speech very quietly, because I am a very modest fellow and detest trouble. I just want to go on and point out that this is class legislation. It will mot give our people faith in our institutions. It will build up bitterness, fear and hatred. We wish to sell our democracy abroad, but if this sort of thing continues we shall not be able to do so. If we are to instil faith in democracy into the peoples of the world: and into our own people we have to feed and: clothe them properly; we have to give them a sense of security, a sense of being a part of Canada. If we do not do this we shall meet more trouble ahead. We shall have to go through all the agonies people have gone through in countries where there have been upheavals. Some of us are trying our best to bring about the change in a peaceful fashion, to bring about a society where real justice and freedom will reign.
At the present time there is one program which would meet the immediate situation. It has been placed on record previously, but I wish to put it on record again. There must be immediate reimposition of price controls on all the basic necessities of life, including food', clothing and fuel; renewal of the subsidies on milk, butter, bread', feed grains, cotton and wool; the closing of the Winnipeg grain exchange and1 the elimination of speculation in essential foods; the restoration of the wartime prices and trade board on a permanent basis in such a manner that it will be able adequately to administer price control; continuation of the excess profits tax, which was discontinued on December 31, 1947; the rationing, if necessary, of any essential commodity which is in short supply, so that all Canadians may get their fair minimum share.

Mr. Speaker, after looking over the geography of Canada, and having something in the backs of our minds which made us think that those who came from Skeena were from a broad and strong part of the country, and would not lend themselves to anything which would not go down very well in the system of those of us who like to think we are strong men of the north, may I say that my conception of Skeena has not been raised very much this evening by the exhibition which I have witnessed, and to which I have listened within the last half hour.
When I think of a loquacious Irish schoolteacher of a decade ago who represented that great constituency in such a charming manner,
{Mr. Green.]
a man who never harmed anymne; then, when I think of the incumbent who immediately preceded the present one, a man who came to this country from Sweden, without a dollar to his name; when I think of his wholesomeness and of the private enterprise in which he took part; -when I think of the example he set to so many who have come to our shores, and how proud we were to know him; and when I think of how we on all sides of the house learned to love him. I must say that tonight I feel let down, after listening to the remarks of the present hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Archibald).
I hope, as he grows a little older, that perhaps he may mature a little. We all do. We do not like to, but we must admit that that maturing does take place. We hope that he will mature, and that he will take a viewpoint of Canada which is much broader than that narrow viewpoint which sets one group of our people against another. I belong to both groups, to the group who work for a living, and to the group who are honoured and privileged to have others working for them-and 1 have working for me several hundred-without strife. I love to know their families and their children, although they have become so numerous that it is not easy to keep track of them.
Yet we have a man rising in his place in (he house and referring to those people as stupid, frustrated little men. I do not hear quite so well now, Mr. Speaker; and when I thought I heard him say that, I thought he was referring to himself. WTe do not want little men-and I do not speak as to stature-* we do not want little men, men small of mind, in this country of ours. Whether they w'eigh 100 or 200 pounds, we want them to be big and broad men; because we have a big country, a broad country, and we are charged by Providence with the responsibility of developing this country for our children. The only ones who can develop it are men who will speak from their hearts and their minds, and will not read into the columns of Hansard theses which perhaps took weeks, or perhaps only a few moments to prepare. I wonder sometimes if those theses are the thoughts of the men who deliver them in the house, or are they the thoughts of others?
Until such time as young men in this honourable house, sir, have something to say which comes from within their own minds, which flows from their breadth of experience, from their reading, from their study, not from some essay handed to them by some outsider, or some outside organization telling them what to say I am wondering if this is really a parlia-

ment. Is it a parliament, or is it a chamber in which the views of others from outside can be placed on the record?
We are in parliament and, according to my idea of things, we speak for our constituents, and for what they think. And if you cannot say what you think, then I doubt very much whether you have a right to be in this chamber.

I am very happy to submit to the suggestion of my learned, honoured and reverend friend. Perhaps the words should not have been used. If they are withdrawn I suppose I shall be in order; I suppose it is a case of whether it was good taste to call someone a stupid, frustrated little man. However, I am the last one that would want to say anything that would disturb any hon. member in this chamber. However, when I listen to someone talking about fifty-five cents a quart when he means 55 cents a hundred pounds I begin to wonder whether he is quite sure what a quart of milk is or what a hundred pounds of milk is. That is what led me to think that perhaps he was not just sure of what it was all about.
Let me get to the subject before us, the speech from the throne, the vehicle which permits us to say something on behalf of our constituents, to make our requests, to tell of some of our difficulties. After having had four constituencies during the last two and a half decades, I think at this stage I might be permitted to say something about my own community.
Before doing so, may I express to the government my great disappointment with regard to the speech from the throne. I am thinking of what was in the minds of the Canadian people when it was presented. I am thinking of the words in the speech from the throne, how it bristled with one outstanding feature, the rise in prices and the high cost of living. My next two or three sentences may be out of order, Mr. Speaker, but I pray your indulgence. When the speech from the throne was introduced the committee on the cost of living was not functioning.
The people of Canada, reading this speech from the throne delivered on December 5, were happy that something would be done. By whom? By their elected representatives. The elected representatives hoped that each would have an. opportunity of saying what he would like to say about this matter. However. that hope is gone because we now have this committee set up. On behalf of the Canadian people I wish every success for the committee.
In what I am going to say now, I call to witness one or two of my hon. friends on the other side. The hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Gladstone) served diligently on a committee day after day and month after month. I wonder what his thoughts are now as to the success of that committee. I wonder what are the thoughts of other hon. members in this chamber who, in days gone by, have served on committees. This committee is simply a stopgap; it is a waste of time. The government waited for something to happen but they were frustrated.
They did not get very far with the department. The staffs of the departments, having been engaged in parliamentary business all their lives, know more than the ordinary member of the House of Commons. Even though members of committees work with great diligence, they are not trained in that particular field. They are unable to match wits with deputy ministers and deputies' deputies and their deputies and their deputies behind them. They have nothing but parliamentary procedure in their blood, and the net result is that this committee will, in my opinion, not be able to give our people the satisfaction they are hoping to get. In the meantime we as members of the house are not able to discharge our responsibility to our people as we would like to discharge it.
What is the cause of some of these difficulties in connection with the austerity program and the loss of exchange and conditions generally? It is the tardiness of the

citizens who are out of pocket $44,000 after an audit, which is the responsibility of this institution, and that they give it consideration in order that we may clear that statement up and be happy about the service which we have been able to render.
I appreciate the opportunity I have had to mention this. I feel a little humble at this time. This is the first time in many years that I have said anything on behalf of my own constituents, and it is the first time in years that I have asked for something on their behalf. I hope that I am one who, when he asks for something, believes he should have it. I say through you, Mr. Speaker, to my hon. friends in the cabinet ajul to those who are responsible in any degree, that anything I have suggested or asked for, I feel I am sound in my request, sound in my judgment; and until such time as they can show reason why they will not acquiesce in these requests, from now until that time, I am determined that some consideration shall be given to the constituency of Danforth.

We derived no less enjoyment from the fruit which he described to us with perfect knowledge and as ably as a painter with his brush. I compliment him for having uttered choice and convincing words first toward the house which he was addressing anti for having spoken with the dignity which characterizes

him, and secondly for having spoken convincing words on behalf of those who do him the honour of electing him as their representative in this house. Those who sit here have no doubt recognized the truth of his allegations and noted the moderation with which he views things and, especially, the eloquence of the words by which he expressed his deep gratitude to the people who have done him the honour I mentioned a few moments ago.
I cannot but make a special mention of the seconder of the address, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey). I listened to him with attention and I especially appreciated what he said in my own language. As we are now going on with the same debate, permit me, Mr. Speaker, to quote the following excerpt from his speech:
Mr. Speaker, my election to this parliament will, I believe, afford me. among other privileges, an exceptional opportunity to appreciate and improve m.v knowledge of fellow citizens whose language I speak with, of course, great difficulty, but among whom, I am happy to say, I have close and valuable friends.
There you have evidence of what broadmindedness is needed to achieve co-operation between the citizens living within the four corners of this wonderful country. I am sure this example will be followed by all those who do not entirely share our views and opinions or who cannot speak our language, so that we may achieve the measure of understanding which we so badly need, which the whole of Canada so deeply needs to remain a great country, to become greater if possible, and to hold the place assigned to it by Providence in the course of past and coming centuries.
The following statement is found in the first paragraph of the speech from the throne:
In many countries, political and social unrest is serious. Failure to agree on peace settlements with Germany and Austria is preventing the recovery of Europe.
No wonder such a situation exists, especially when, in many countries, the powers that be entirely lack good faith and, instead of striving to spread among the nations of the world a spirit of goodwill necessary for an enduring peace, seek rather to promote a dubious philosophy, philosophy they seek to spread the world over, so as to achieve an aim envisioned by the followers of that theory since its inception: to crush under its iron heel humanity which yearns only for peace and mutual understanding.

The Address-Mr. P. Gauthier
We are surprised at the delay in the signing of peace treaties. But such delay is only normal. See what is happening in Europe and in several countries I could mention. After the war, Russia got more in the way of war reparations than was obtained by any other allied country from the nations which fought under the swastika. Russia received larger reparations than some countries which have probably suffered more than she did. Further, not content with accepting, taking, extracting from these countries the amount of money required, Russia bleeds them white, throws their industries out of gear, undermines their culture and, to reward them, tries to spread within their borders the questionable philosophy of communism which I mentioned at the beginning of my speech. Such is the reward bestowed by the hammer and sickle.
Another paragraph of the speech from the throne reads as follows:
In view of the price fixed for the 1948-1949 crop year under the wheat agreement with the United Kingdom, you will be asked to consider a measure to provide for an increase in the initial payment to producers.
If my understanding is correct, this means that we will be asked to pay western wheat growers a certain sum of money because under the British agreement they did not get a fair price for their wheat. The eastern farmers will be good fellows as usual and, through their representatives who will co-operate with the western members, they will compensate those who claim that they have been plundered-strong language, perhaps, but this is how I feel at present. As I say, we shall be good fellows, but I hope that when the time comes to take steps that will benefit our Eastern farmers and workers, those same Western farmers will also be good fellows by asking their representatives to act as we did, and will not hesitate to comfort our farmers with grateful words. The Western farmers will understand that if they sometimes find themselves in a critical position, the Eastern farmers also have to cope with similar difficulties, especially as far as the dairy industry is concerned. In that connection, we hope our farmers will receive the same consideration as Western producers.

I quote another paragraph found in the speech from the throne:
You will be asked to consider plans for a low rental housing project for veterans.
This I fully endorse, Mr. Speaker. I feel that our veterans are entitled to every consideration since they risked everything to save democracy and Christianity as well as to prevent national socialist or fascist ideas from taking root in our country. Heaven grant that we be spared the need of resorting to similar methods in order to stop communist ideas from spreading in our country, following the activities we have uncovered and which I shall discuss again later. However, we must think not only of our veterans but of the rest of the population, of all those who are homeless.
At long last, let them build homes for our people. In the province of Quebec, especially, veterans as others, have families of five to ten children or more. What good, therefore, are those tiny postwar houses? Despite the legislation designed to promote harmony between industry and labour and between large and small farm producers, true co-operation will not be achieved among our people unless they are provided with decent shelters for their families. Many of the dwellings built after the war are by far too small for large families. Why not be realistic? Thank God, in the province of Quebec large families are not and will not for a long time yet be things of the past. We are not depending upon immigration to increase our population and, as I said before, we need houses large enough to provide our families with a decent standard of living.

Let me read another paragraph of the speech from the throne:
A measure similar to the one introduced at the last session of parliament to provide more effective machinery for the adjustment of differences between employers and employees will be submitted for your consideration.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, if recrimination on the part of both employers and employees is of the kind we have been hearing tonight, such co-operation is very unlikely to prevail. I am not used to hearing very bitter discussions between industrialists in my county, and I am grateful for it.
My constituency is half-agricultural, halfindustrial. I believe that the agricultural element is the larger of the two, but nevertheless one will find there a mining region which is unfortunately closed down as an aftermath of the war. The quarrying industry is flourishing in two districts, at Riviere-a-Pierre and Saint Marc, whence comes the limestone of which I have spoken. Portneuf has roofing nnd kraft paper industries at Portneuf Station and at Pont Rouge, plus two newsprint plants, one at Saint Raymond, the other at Donna-cona.
We are not used to strikes in my constituency. To my knowledge, we have had but one strike. That lasted one week and was settled to the satisfaction of both parties, as far as I know.
I do not remember any strike ever having taken place at Saint Raymond. There was one at Donnacona, and it lasted only one day. At the present time I may say that the lowest salary paid there, that is to the labourer, is 85 cents per hour. The most perfect co-operation exists between industry and labour. We have but one labour union, the "syndicats catholiques" which, I believe, have more than 800 members. There is perfect agreement between the company's management, civil
cause-I say so with some reluctance but with the knowledge that it is true

because there and church authorities and labour leaders. The company even affords advantages to those workers who wish to join the union. Why does it do so, some one may ask? Simply because before letting any disagreement come to a head, they meet, negotiate and manage to come to terms. Strikes do not occur when things are done that way.
Why do not like conditions always prevail in other parts of this country? Simply be-are people who profit from strikes, who seek to divert workers from their jobs by turning them against their employers, because it fits in with their design-I do not hesitate to say it-their design to foment revolution. That is perhaps premature in Canada; I sincerely hope so, but in other countries, talk of revolution was sometimes thought premature but it burst upon them like a hail-storm.
At Donnacona or anywhere else in my riding, there are no trouble-makers, in other words no communists. That is why we have no strikes. We have people who were not born in our constituency, people who were born in other countries. They are not troublemakers, they are good citizens who get along well with native Canadians. Why? Because they do not entertain dubious philosophies, because they know they have the right to work, and they are not unaware that if they have rights, they also have duties to perform.

The latter, which they had obtained in England, were English passports illegally secured in the name of British subjects born in the British isles; and, with such spurious passports, these illegal immigrants violated this land of ours and well intended to remain here. I have here a picture taken from the Montreal Gazette of February 13, 1948. Am accompanying article tells of the seizure by provincial and city police of certain documents, lottery tickets which show that the communist party is not to be found only in Moscow or in the Cominform, the new organization set up in lieu of the Comintern. Those lottery tickets came from Italy. This picture shows first Tim Buck, of Toronto, leader of the Labour Progressive party, and, just under, one of those lottery tickets, the proceeds of which were to be used) for the consolidation of the Italian republic. Lower down, I read these words which I translate as I go along: "This subscription is in favour of the Italian communist party to promote elections to the national assembly. In spite of my limited knowledge of the Italian language, I can give a literal translation. We are fully justified, Mr. Speaker, in asking that the Immigration Department or division be more adamant in these matters. Those lottery tickets were surely smuggled somehow into Canada. In Montreal, they were distributed in several places. There is evidence that the communist party is supplying funds for the Italian elections next April. Are we not justified in asking the authorities, federal, provincial and municipal to be on the alert and to work untiringly in order to unearth the subversive propaganda with which we are literally swamped in Canada? I am not afraid to
The Address-Mr. Stanfield

speak frankly. Those documents have been seized, but how many more are circulating ini the country and ini our homes.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that any or all of our government authorities will not stop investigating nor relax their vigilance and thus spare themselves our censure for their guilty weakness and apathy. In 1937, when I mentioned communist activities in this country, all I got was more or less derisive laughter from the house. That happened just a little over ten years ago and yet, today, in Canada, we find a communist party that styles itself labour progressive. What matters, however, is not its name but the fact that it has recognized leaders and is extremely active. I do not claim that we should ban these radicals in order to curb the party's activities in the most effective fashion, but I do contend that we must be well acquainted with the communist theory in order to fight it successfully. For Christians, the best way to oppose communism is to live a Christian life. We must not hesitate, even in public, to show that we are Christians, nor must we refrain from studying this questionable philosophy, for when we have become familiar with it, we shall be better equipped to fight it, the weapon of knowledge being even more effective than that of legislation.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I should like, first of all, to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address in reply upon the able manner in which they acquitted themselves. I am sure,

if one may judge from their contribution to this debate, they have bright futures in the political life of our country.
Much has been said in this debate about wheat and hogs. In fact, some nights when I go home I fear that I shall dream of hogs and wheat. Therefore this evening I feel that I would be justified for a few moments if I were to set out the merits of the old province of Nova Scotia, and' to say something about the fine people who live by the sea.
Nova Scotia is a pleasant spot indeed in which to live; and the people who live there are the finest to be found anywhere on this globe. They live ini a very happy and pleasant way. Contrary to what many people think, especially to what you may read in some papers, most Nova Scotians live in lovely homes. They are proud of their homes and they take great interest ini them. They have civic pride in their properties and they keep them in) the best repair possible. I think the homes in Nova Scotia compare favourably with those ini any other part of Canada.
The people of Nova Scotia enjoy life. They do not chase the dollar quite as hard as do the people of Ontario and Quebec. When they want to go fishing, they go fishing; when they want to play golf, they play golf; when they want to dance, they go to a dance, and they have the privilege of dancing with as many beautiful, gifted and charming ladies as there are any place else in the world.
A lot of people think that we are paupers there, that we are poor financially. I am quite willing to admit that there are other parts of the world which are more prosperous than we are, that possess more of this world's goods, but those people do not enjoy life any more than we do. We have never had to ask for a great deal of assistance. I should like to point out to some of these western bronchos who do so much talking about wheat and hogs that a few years ago when the price of wheat and hogs was not so high as it has been of late years many of the towns in Nova Scotia sent carload after carload of clothing and other things out to the people who were suffering from such hard times in the west. We have a great fondness for western Canada because many Nova Scotians have gone out there to settle.
The people of Nova Scotia are very thrifty and conservative by nature. You understand, sir, that I use the word "conservative" to denote their thriftiness, not their politics. We in Nova Scotia are proud of our educational system. We have Dalhousie University; we have Acadia University and we have St.

The Address-Mr. Stanfield
Francis Xavier University. Then there is King's College, which is really affiliated with Dalhousie. We educate our people down there in order that they can help to build up the rest of the world. Perhaps it is too bad that many of our people leave the province, but Nova Scotians are great people to roam. They like to go away and see the world. Everywhere you go you will find Nova Scotians and you will find also that most of them have done very well indeed.
Just a word about our countryside, our picturesque scenery. We have heard a great deal about the scenery in Ontario and British Columbia, but I do not think the countryside of Nova Scotia has to take a back seat to any area. Let me tell you that it makes you feel good to be alive to take a drive along the Dartmouth lakes on a fine, bright autumn afternoon, when the leaves of the hardwood trees have turned to red. Then there is another lovely drive from Hawkesbury to Hastings. When you go through there in the evening just as the sun is about to set you would almost think you were in Switzerland. Then there is another lovely scenic drive around Cabot trail. I think all who have taken that drive will agree that the scenery is picturesque. In fact our province is just one picture after another. I invite those who do not believe me to come down to see for themselves.
The climate of Nova Scotia is quite bad in the spring and we can offer no excuses. We are not very proud of that weather, but for the other nine months of the year the climate is most delightful. At times it may have its drawbacks, but most of the time it will compare favourably with the climate in any other part of the world, yes, even in Ottawa.
We have good roads in Nova Scotia. Perhaps we have to thank the Liberal government for them. I hate to do it, but that is the fact. All our main trunk roads are paved with asphalt. We have no four-lane highways like there are in Ontario and Quebec, but our main roads are all paved and our secondary roads are rapidly being paved. The province of Nova Scotia is a natural set-up for the tourist trade.
It may be said that we have not sufficient tourist accommodation in the province. Let me mention some of the best. There is a grand summer hotel at White Point beach; then there is The Pines at Digby, and then (here is the Keltic Lodge in Cape Breton. Those tourist resorts are as fine as you will find any place, and we are proud of them. Additional hotels and tourist camps are being
erected all the time. I am certain that Nova Scotia has a very bright future as far as the tourist trade is concerned, and in saying that I am not forgetting that we have enjoyed a very good tourist business in the past. However, with our good roads, our lovely climate and our hospitable people, I am sure our tourist business will continue to grow.
As I said before, I realize that perhaps there are more prosperous places in Canada than Nova Scotia, and I should like to point out a few ways in which I think our province could be helped to better its economic position. I am not one of those who believe that Nova Scotia should not have entered confederation. I believe our place is in confederation, but perhaps we should have received better treatment. Some of the fault may lie with ourselves because we are not as aggressive as we might be; but, be that as it may, we have not received as much consideration as we should1 have.
For instance, in order to get to the island of Cape Breton you have to cross about a mile of water. There are about 150,000 people on the island of Cape Breton and they have to go back and forth on a ferryboat. I believe, and so do most Nova Scotians, that a bridge should be built across the strait of Canso to connect the island of Cape Breton with the mainland. It is my belief that if 150,000 people were living on an island in lake Ontario, separated from the mainland by only a mile of water, they would have had a bridge long ago. We may be told that it would cost a lot of money to build that bridge because of the swiftness of the water and ice conditions in the spring of the year. That is true, but I am sure that the difficulties are not insuperable, and bridges have been built over harder places than the strait of Canso. Suppose it does cost $15,000,000. Today we have become so accustomed to talking in terms of hundreds of millions of dollars that $15,000,000 in comparison seems very small.
I would also suggest to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) that a faster train service be provided between Montreal and Halifax. I know you cannot change geography, but the time can be shortened that it takes a train to go from Montreal to Halifax. I realize that the roadbed from Montreal to Halifax is not as good as that between Montreal and Chicago and that the Halifax train cannot, therefore, make as fast time, but I have a suggestion to make to the minister which would speed up the service. Instead of running three trains around to Campbellton
The Address-Mr. Stanfield

and away down the St. Lawrence river, I suggest that one train, after it leaves Moncton, be routed' over the Grand Trunk Pacific and go through Fredericton, Edmundston and on to Montreal. I understand that this route would shorten the running time by four or five hours between Montreal and Halifax. I would also point out that the people of Fredericton and Edmundston and all the way along that line have a very poor train service to Montreal, just as poor as anything could be. If my suggestions were adopted, not only would the running time between Montreal and Halifax be shortened by four or five hours, but these places which I mentioned would have a first-class rail service to and from Montreal. The other two trains could run over the present route to serve that traffic. I believe that the people of Moncton and the province of Nova Scotia are entitled to ask the Minister of Transport to look carefully into this suggestion to see if it is not feasible.
There is one subject on which there has been no discussion at all in this house, and it is that of our great forest industry and allied industries. It comes next in importance to agriculture combined with our dairying industry. I realize that our forests are in the care of the province, but still it is the duty of every citizen of Canada-and this house is a very important body of Canadian citizens- to look after the welfare of our forests. The forests of Nova Scotia have been greatly depleted in the last twenty years; yet they are of untold value to our province; and, while selective cutting, reforestation and the care of our forests are in the hands of the provincial government, it is my conviction that this government should do everything it can to foster and speed up the care of our forests. They are the second greatest form of wealth we have across Canada and are being depleted by fire, insects and ruthless cutting. The forests are vanishing more quickly than they should be. But with proper cutting and reforestation practices we would have in Nova Scotia enough lumber to last us forever. I think 500,000,000 feet of lumber are being cut lately every year, besides pulpwood, hardwood, et cetera, from the forests of our province. If we took as good care of our forests as Sweden and other countries do, our children would never need to worry about the income to be derived from the forest wealth of our province.
There is another way in which our province could be helped. The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black) has been speaking on behalf of the marshlands for many years. These lands have practically gone to waste,

from many causes into which I shall not go at the moment. But when you see elsewhere in the province small farms being settled on land suitable for growing only a few spruce trees and then see those rich marshlands flooded out and the buildings falling down on the adjacent upland, with only a few cattle here and there trying to pick up a living, I sometimes wonder what is the matter. The marshlands cannot be reclaimed by the settlers or farmers themselves because it takes heavy machinery to do it. In the old days that work was all done by hand. In 1750, the Tant.ra-mar marshes under the French settlers were built. They were assisted by prison labour brought out from France. They did not know what a steam shovel was; all they had was oxen and a hand shovel. But today we have bulldozers and all the necessary equipment for rehabilitating those marshlands. I am afraid, however, that the marshlands constitute more or less of a political football, and I am not blaming the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), because I believe he is sympathetic toward rehabilitating those lands.
I should like to say a word or two on the deficiency of the United States dollar, a situation into which we run every ten or twelve years. I believe we should have a long-term national policy whereby we could make in Canada a great many of the articles we now import from the United States, thereby building up our country and providing more employment for our people. May I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that some of these industries be established in Nova Scotia. We shall welcome the help of the dominion government in having new industries established in our province. Somebody may say that these industries could not be run down there. I should like to point out that in Nova Scotia there are many industries which have prospered for many years and sold their products across this fair land of ours. I can assure this house that industry can be run profitably in Nova Scotia. Therefore I would ask the house to lend us its support to see if some of these industries cannot be established in Nova Scotia to make the products that we have been buying across the border so that the deficiency in United States dollars will not keep on recurring.
I think I have spoken for twenty minutes, Mr. Speaker, and that is a long time for me; therefore I shall take my seat.

It was amusing to me to
read an editorial in his own paper, the Halifax Chronicle, printed on the day that he made his speech in the house. I think I should put it on the record, because it does not bear out what the hon. member said here. In fact it says this:
Some Cheer Would be Welcome
In his press interview of last week end the Rinht Hon. C. D. Howe ran the gamut of the political octave in respect to Nova Scotia with remarkable optimism, and made a number of very plain statements. Specifically, to the question as to whether he had anything to say to cheer the citizens of Halifax, in view of the prevailing unemployment situation, the Minister of Trade and Commerce queried whether any cheer is necessary and suggested that a considerable number of our unemployed -are seasonal workers who have -alternative means of getting a living when their normal trade is slack.
National employment service here could probably disillusion Mr. Howe on this point. There are, admittedly, odd jobs here and there that men can take. But they do not fill the dinner pail, and they come nowhere ne-ar to the point of absorbing even temporarily the total number of unemployed. Over the week end, according to officials of the freight handlers' union, not a single stevedore or freight-handler was employed on the waterfront at the time of year when work should be most plentiful. A lack of steel has thrown many out of work at the shipyards. Men with skills such -as these unemployed have -are hardly the types that ought to be set to work shovelling snow. That is like putting an unemployed architect to work laying bricks.
The trouble at bottom is that, while these men are losing work, the province is in some danger of losing industries which have been built up painfully during the war. That is not merely a local problem. It is one which, if not rectified soon, will have permanent repercussions on various branches of industry all over the country in the future. It is the part of wise statesmanship to foresee such tendencies and to take steps to forestall them. Mere optimism will solve none of our problems here or elsewhere. We need wise planning and fast action.
That is exactly what the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) was suggesting in this house. To solve some of the problems in that part of the country, it is necessary to take action and to take action immediately. The sen-ior member for Halifax said that certain- western members had gone to the maritimes to tell the farmers there how to make money. I can- assure the hon-. member that the farmers of the maritimes know their business quite well enough without having to take any advice from farmers from any other part of the country. They are quite efficient in- their methods of operation. If they had n-ot been- they would not have stayed in- business during the thirties.
In my conversations with farmers in the maritimes, I found- them very much the same as farmers all over Canada. All they ask for is an even break in this economy of ours, and they are prepared to d'o their bit in providing the food that is necessary. They, along with farmers all- over Canada, are anxious about the present situation. When they find that ceilings have been placed on the goods which they have to sell, while no controls are placed over many of the things they have to buy, is it not enough for the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to rise in his place and say, as he did- the other day, that we have in this country a guarantee in the form of an Agricultural Prices Support Act that will guarantee in the future that agricultural prices will be maintained at a stable level. The Minister of Agriculture said as reported at page 807 of Hansard the other day:
The policy which protects the consumer is sound because we have said in the prices support legislation that if the time ever comes when the bottom falls out of prices we will ask every taxpayer in this country to help -to the extent provided in the Agricultural Prices Support Act. that is, $200 million, to maintain -the price levels.
The Minister of Agriculture knows quite well that is an act set up for the purpose of maintaining floor prices under agricultural products during the transitional period; it sets out quite clearly in the act that it is an act to protect prices during the transitional period from war to peace. When these subsidies are all removed and we are through the transitional period, at the very time when it will be necessary to give some support to agriculture this act, according to its own words which will be found in another place in Hansard, will be

The Address

Mr. Wright

ultra vires, if maintained at any other time than during the transitional period. That is one of the points which we in this group have been urging on the government. We have been asking them to make this legislation permanent legislation and provide that these floor prices will be maintained when they are needed.
On motion of Mr. Wright the debate was adjourned.

Mr. ST. LAURENT: I know the Minister of Finance is ready on Monday with both Bill No. 3 and Bill No. 7, dealing with the gold subsidy. There have been requests from many members of the house on both sides that the
latter bill be taken up at an early date. The Minister of Finance is not here today. He had official duties that called him elsewhere, and I am soriy not to be able to say in which order he intends to proceed, but he is ready with both of them for Monday. I hope that the order which he will select will be one that will be convenient to hon. members.

Either Bill No. 3 or Bill No. 7?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Both are ready. There were some hopes that both might be disposed of, but I am not able to say which order he will prefer.
